partners.name: Cycubix

asked.by: Dinis, met at the summit; relayed by attendees.1.fringe@PrompTugal.dinis

partners.one_line: A Dublin cybersecurity and GRC consultancy and training company; its first product, ConsentScan, scans websites for cookie and consent violations, with an MCP server on its Pro plan.

public.fact: Cycubix offers cybersecurity training (secure coding in several languages, threat modeling, secure coding for AI and LLM applications against the OWASP Top 10 for LLMs) and consultancy (risk reviews, ISO 27001, GDPR, SOC, NIS2, vCISO).
ConsentScan, by Cycubix Ltd, Dublin, is a GDPR and ePrivacy cookie consent checker: one free scan with no sign-up, about 4 minutes, graded A to F.
A scan loads the site like a first-time EU visitor, records what fires before consent, then clicks Reject and checks whether trackers keep firing.
ConsentScan started as a check Cycubix ran during its ISO 27001, GDPR and security engagements.

Plans: Free (1 scan); Starter €19 a month (1 monitored domain); Pro €39 a month (3 monitored domains, and an MCP server to run scans from Claude, Cursor or any MCP client); Agency €99 (10 domains); Enterprise on request.

Its EU Consent Index (2 Nov 2026) tested 160 leading websites in eight EU countries: 69% loaded trackers or non-essential cookies before consent, and 58% of the sites where a Reject click could be completed kept tracking afterwards.

told: Both sides agreed the public company information can be published as a case study.

help.pitch: ConsentScan measures the gap between what a site says (its consent banner) and what it does (the trackers that fire). RiskMandate measures the same kind of gap for AI agents: what an agent was asked to do against what it can reach. For ConsentScan's own agentic workflow and its MCP server, RiskMandate would write down the mandate, measure the reach and record the gap.
mandate: The scanner's own job: load a site, record cookies, click Reject, grade. A narrow, writable mandate.
reach: Its MCP server lets Claude, Cursor or any MCP client run scans: an outside agent with a tool. What the MCP server's credentials can reach beyond scanning is unknown from public pages.
gap: Unknown from public pages; the mandate is narrow, so the gap is measurable. 'Installed, not blocking' (its words for consent platforms) is the same shape as an agent policy that exists but is not enforced.

partners.one_line: An AI cloud platform: AI agents work in a scoped, isolated workspace on a project's source, and Adios builds, previews and hosts the result, without giving the agent the platform.

public.fact: Describes itself as an AI cloud platform for developers and founders to build with AI agents, review source changes, and deploy and operate applications, APIs, databases and workflows. Its legal name is Adios Global LLC.
Claude, Cursor, Codex or ChatGPT connect to Adios over MCP; Adios builds the app in an isolated cloud workspace, gives a preview, and puts it live with HTTPS when the user approves.

An agent connects to one selected workspace 'without receiving a general browser shell or platform credentials'; every action is narrowed to that team and workspace, through scoped file, Git, task, preview and log operations.

Its stated principle: 'Give the agent enough context to work, without giving it the platform.' Agent activity stays tied to the workspace it affected, with diffs, task output, previews and logs for review.

Runtime controls: restricted runtime sandboxes with Linux namespaces, cgroups and resource limits where the runtime supports them; secrets as secret:// references resolved only for the build or runtime path that needs them; tenant boundaries through platform APIs.
Its security page says SOC 2 and ISO 27001 work is underway and the reports are not final yet.
Named customers on its site run on Adios: one moved its frontend and backend from Kubernetes on AWS, one runs workflows and agents, one deploys prototypes to production.
Plans start with a free workspace; always-on hosting from $10 a month.

told: Its environment runs agents under controls that greatly reduce their reach and blast radius.

help.pitch: Adios shrinks what an agent can reach: one workspace, scoped operations, no platform credentials, secrets resolved only where needed. RiskMandate measures exactly that difference: the mandate (what the agent should do), the reach (what it can actually do), and the gap. Run the same agent bare and on Adios, and the shrinking gap is the business case, measured and evidenced.
mandate: A declared task in a selected workspace: edit these files, run this task, return a reviewable change. That is a written mandate.
reach: On Adios, by its own pages: one workspace, scoped tools, no general shell or platform credentials, secrets resolved per path. On a developer's laptop, the same agent reaches everything the developer can.
gap: Unknown in numbers until measured. Our measurement would put a figure on how much reach Adios removes per agent, against the same task run without it.

partners.name: TestMu AI

asked.by: Dinis, at their stand at the summit; relayed by attendees.1.fringe@PrompTugal.dinis

partners.one_line: An agentic AI quality engineering platform (formerly LambdaTest). Its Agent Assurance and Rook CLI test AI agents that act, and grade them on what they actually changed, not on what they say they did.

public.fact: TestMu AI (formerly LambdaTest; legal entity LambdaTest, Inc.; renamed 12 January 2026) is an agentic AI quality engineering platform that 'assures AI deployments across the enterprise and the real world'.
Agent Assurance tests how AI agents that act (call tools, write files, hit APIs) actually behave, including coding, workflow, back-office and multi-agent systems.

Rook CLI reads the codebase to find the agent, writes functional and adversarial scenarios, runs them against the live agent, and grades each criterion from evidence: Pass, Fail and Unable to Verify are counted separately.

'Agent Assurance does not grade the agent on what it says it did': recorded tool calls, command output, exit status, changed files, artifacts and read-only verification carry the verdict; the agent's own reply is the weakest signal.
Its documentation says: 'Rook does not sandbox or roll back the agent under test. Refunds, emails, tickets, database updates, and filesystem writes happen in the target environment.'
Self-serve, with a 14-day free trial for new organisations; Rook's public release repository is on GitHub with sample agents that have real defects to find.

It lists SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 certifications, offices in San Francisco, Noida, Bengaluru and Dubai, and a Leader position in the 2026 Gartner Magic Quadrant for Agentic Software Quality Assurance Platforms.

told: Agent Assurance became generally available in late October 2026 and reports an 'assurance gap' for results it could not verify (relayed from its press release; not yet read by us).
Rook plugs into CI: GitHub Actions, Jenkins, Argo CD (relayed; not yet read by us).
Its CEO spoke at the summit on 11 November: 'When AI verifies AI'.

help.pitch: TestMu AI proves what an agent did. RiskMandate defines and measures what an agent may do (its mandate and its reach), and our harness enforces it (ABP policies, run reports). Together: policy, then enforcement, then proof. Its own documentation names the seam: Rook does not sandbox the agent under test, so the actions are real. A mandate and a harness are what make that safe.
mandate: Rook writes scenarios and criteria for an agent; an ABP policy states what the agent may do. Our policies could be Rook's criteria.
reach: Rook grades observed effects (tool calls, file changes, API calls) in the target environment. What the agent could have reached beyond those effects is what RiskMandate measures.
gap: Its 'Unable to Verify' (and the assurance gap it reports) is the gap between claim and proof; ours is the gap between mandate and reach. Two halves of one record.

together.title: A joint pilot
together.text: Run Rook against one of our own agents, under its ABP policy, and set Rook's verdicts beside our run report: what it was allowed to do, what it could reach, what it provably did.
